name: Dutch Defense: Stonewall Variation
summary: The Stonewall Dutch builds a d5-e6-f5 pawn wall gripping e4 and aims at a kingside attack, at the cost of a passive light-squared bishop.
intro: The Stonewall Variation is the classical, structurally committed branch of the Dutch Defence, reached after moves such as 1.d4 f5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 e6 4.Nf3 d5 5.O-O Bd6 6.c4 c6. Black erects a fixed pawn chain on d5, e6 and f5 that clamps down on the e4-square and lays the foundation for a direct kingside attack. In return Black accepts a permanent structural concession: a backward e-pawn and a notoriously passive light-squared bishop.
line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 e6 Nf3 d5 O-O Bd6 c4 c6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Stonewall is built around a rigid pawn formation on c6, d5, e6 and f5 that gives Black an iron grip on the e4-square and a durable, hard-to-crack kingside. With the light squares in the centre firmly controlled, Black's whole strategy points toward the enemy king: the dark-squared bishop drops to the active d6-square, the queen swings to the kingside via ...Qe8-h5, and a knight often lands on the outpost at e4. The classic attacking mechanism combines pressure down the b8-h2 diagonal with a knight on e4 and rook lifts, aiming to overwhelm White's castled position.

The price of this structure is real and permanent. The e6-pawn is backward and the e5-square is a hole that White can occupy with a knight, and above all the light-squared bishop is hemmed in behind its own pawns, giving Black a chronic 'bad bishop'. Much of Black's manoeuvring is therefore devoted to solving this problem, most commonly by rerouting the bishop with ...Bd7-e8-h5 to bring it into the kingside attack, or by ...b6 and ...Ba6 to trade it off. White, meanwhile, targets the weak central complex, angling to establish a knight on e5 or the c5-square, to exchange the dark-squared bishop that guards Black's kingside, and to open the position where the bad bishop tells.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The modern main line features the flexible bishop placement ...Bd6, which supports the ...e5 and ...f4 breaks and keeps the piece aimed at White's kingside, in contrast to the older set-ups with the bishop on e7. Black's central plan is the manoeuvre ...Bd7-e8-h5 to activate the problem bishop, together with ...Qe8, ...Ne4 and rook lifts to build the attack. White frequently answers with b3 and Ba3, seeking to exchange the important d6-bishop, and with Nbd2 or Ne5 to fight for the key central squares.

White's principal try is to prove that the light-square strategy leaves lasting weaknesses. A standard plan is Qc2, b3, Ba3 and Rac1, contesting the dark-squared bishop and pressing on the c-file, often combined with the space-gaining c4-c5 to fix Black's weaknesses and gain queenside room. Black must decide between an all-out kingside attack with ...g5-g4 and the more positional route of freeing the game with a well-timed ...e5 or ...dxc4. The recurring tension is clear: White works on the queenside and the light-square weaknesses, while Black races to generate a mating attack before those long-term factors become decisive.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Stonewall is one of the oldest recognised attacking systems, its name evoking the immovable wall of pawns that characterises the structure, and versions of it were played in the nineteenth century by masters seeking a straightforward plan of attack against the castled king. The modern treatment, with the bishop developed to d6 rather than e7, was refined in the twentieth century and gave the variation new life by improving Black's attacking chances and easing the bad-bishop problem. It has been adopted as a practical winning weapon by a number of leading grandmasters who appreciate its clear strategic aims. Today the Stonewall Dutch is respected as a solid yet ambitious system, offering Black a coherent middlegame plan at the cost of accepting well-defined structural risks.

keyIdeas: The d5-e6-f5-c6 pawn wall gives Black a firm grip on the e4-square.
Black aims for a kingside attack with ...Bd6, ...Qe8-h5 and ...Ne4.
The backward e-pawn and the e5-hole are Black's structural liabilities.
The light-squared bishop is a chronic problem piece for Black.
Black reroutes it via ...Bd7-e8-h5 or trades it with ...b6 and ...Ba6.
White targets the c5/e5 squares and the weak central light-square complex.

white: Occupy the e5- and c5-squares with a well-supported knight.
Play b3, Ba3 and Rac1 to trade Black's active d6-bishop and press the c-file.
Advance c4-c5 to gain queenside space and fix Black's weaknesses.
Exploit the backward e6-pawn and the hole on e5 in the long run.
Open the position to make Black's bad light-squared bishop tell.
black: Clamp the centre with the d5-e6-f5 pawn wall and control e4.
Launch a kingside attack with ...Qe8-h5, ...Ne4 and rook lifts.
Activate the problem bishop via the ...Bd7-e8-h5 manoeuvre.
Alternatively trade the bad bishop with ...b6 and ...Ba6.
Consider the ...g5-g4 pawn storm to open lines against the king.
